hints: Think about what you actually measure in this experiment, a time for a fixed amount of $\text{OH}^-$ to be used up, and what quantity divided by time gives a rate.
walkthrough:
Link rate to a measurable change**
Imagine sitting with the stopwatch in this experiment. You start with pink alkaline solution and you wait until the pink disappears. That time tells you how quickly $0.0010 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ is consumed. So rate is always amount changed divided by time taken.
Final answer: Rate of reaction is the change in amount (or concentration) of reactant or product with time (per unit time).

hints: Recall what $E_a$ means on the molecular energy axis and which side of that line represents molecules energetic enough for successful collision.
walkthrough:
Read what the axes and $E_a$ tell you**
The y-axis is proportion of molecules, the x-axis is molecular energy. The mark $E_a$ is the minimum energy needed for reaction on collision. Only molecules to the right of that line have $E \ge E_a$.

Identify the area**
The proportion is not a single point, it is the whole tail of the distribution. So you shade the small area under the curve from $E_a$ to the right, out along the energy axis.
Final answer: Shade or label the area under the curve to the right of $E_a$ (energy greater than or equal to $E_a$).

hints: Think about what heating from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ does to average molecular energy and to the spread of energies.
Remember the two sketch rules for a higher T curve: where it must start, and how peak height and peak position change while keeping total area constant.
walkthrough:
Picture what heating does to molecules**
At $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ every molecule on average moves faster. Very few molecules still have near zero energy, so the curve must still start at the origin. The most probable energy moves to a higher value, so the peak shifts right.

Keep the number of molecules the same**
You have the same sample, just hotter. Total area under the curve must stay the same. If the distribution spreads over a wider energy range, the peak must drop lower to keep area constant. The new curve therefore starts at the origin, rises below the original at first, then crosses it once after the original peak and stays above it in the high energy tail.

Final answer: New curve starts at origin, peak shifted to the right (higher energy) and lower than original; curve crosses original once only, beyond the peak of the original, and stays above original at high energy with same total area.

hints: Decide whether $E_a$ is a property of the reaction pathway or a property of the molecules, and whether heating changes the energy barrier itself.
walkthrough:
Separate barrier from molecules**
$E_a$ is the minimum energy needed for the bond breaking step. Heating gives more molecules enough energy to clear that barrier, which is why the tail area in (b)(i) grows, but it does not lower the height of the barrier itself. Only a catalyst or a different reaction pathway changes $E_a$.
Final answer: No change / none. $E_a$ is unchanged by temperature.

hints: Look at the structure $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$, a tertiary bromoalkane, and recall whether bulky tertiary substrates favour one step or two steps with a carbocation.
Think about the polarity of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and where the first curly arrow must start and finish to form the intermediate.
Consider how the $\text{OH}^-$ ion attacks in the second step, which atom donates the lone pair and which carbon accepts it.
walkthrough:
Spot why this is SN1**
You have 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$. The carbon attached to Br is joined to three methyl groups, so it is tertiary. It is too crowded for direct backside attack and it can form a stable tertiary carbocation, so the reaction goes in two steps by unimolecular substitution.

Draw slow ionisation to the carbocation**
Show $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ because Br is more electronegative than C. Draw a curly arrow starting on the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair and pointing onto Br (or just beyond it) to give $\text{Br}^-$ and the planar intermediate $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$. Put the full positive charge on the central carbon.

Draw fast attack by hydroxide**
Now show $\text{OH}^-$ with its lone pairs and negative charge on O. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on O to the positively charged central carbon of the $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ intermediate to form $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

Final answer: Step 1: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ + \text{Br}^-$ with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$. Step 2: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ with curly arrow from lone pair on O of $\text{OH}^-$ to central C of carbocation. Intermediate is tert-butyl cation $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$.

hints: Focus on what $\text{OH}^-$ is, an electron pair donor, and what happens to Br, it is replaced by OH.
walkthrough:
Name what the nucleophile does**
$\text{OH}^-$ is a nucleophile, it donates an electron pair to the electron deficient carbon. The Br is substituted by OH, so the overall type is nucleophilic substitution, here by the unimolecular $S_N1$ route.

hints: Use the table trend, shorter time means faster rate, and predict whether the chloroalkane will be faster or slower than the bromoalkane.
Compare the strength of the bond broken in the slow step, $\text{C-Cl}$ versus $\text{C-Br}$, and link bond strength to $E_a$ and rate.
walkthrough:
Connect time to rate**
The pink phenolphthalein disappears when all $\text{OH}^-$ is consumed. A longer time means a slower reaction. The slow step in (c)(i) is breaking the carbon halogen bond to form the carbocation.

Compare bond strengths**
Cl is smaller than Br, so the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is shorter and stronger than $\text{C-Br}$ and needs more energy to break. That gives a higher $E_a$, fewer molecules can react per second at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, so the rate falls and you wait longer for the pink colour to disappear.

Final answer: Time taken increases (longer time for pink to disappear, slower rate) because the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is stronger than the $\text{C-Br}$ bond, so more energy / higher $E_a$ is needed to break it.
